cable
fincrime

The only fincrime startup with a live product at the time I joined.

It’s a very niche market (probably the most niche I’ve ever worked in) which came with it’s own set of challenges in terms of user feedback, and competitive analysis. Luckily we had two amazing experts on the team that I leaned on heavily for product research, whilst iterating and maturing the first version of our product.

Having been on the initial stage of multiple projects, I’m comfortable in working with what’s available — iterating and testing with big and well informed steps, or smaller more exploratory and tentative ones. As the sole designer at Cable I was happy to discover that the few companies that were on board with us, were extremely available and keen to help us help them. This was a welcome addition, in informing my product decisions during the development of our second and third versions.

The existing product when I joined, had essentially one feature. And had been stuck there for a bit, due to what seemed to me, as self imposed constraints from poorly informed early decisions.

v0.1

Dissecting v0.1

Overly generous white space.

Two menu bars.

Content lives “inside” the rows which requires expanding the view, pushing other info out of view.

Flows are triggered too far apart.

This may have a been a well intended effort to have both overall Paper Trails view, and individually interact with them, but as the product needed to grow, it became a limiting factor.

v1.0

By creating more views, we reduced complexity.

There was now a home page for Paper Trails, which sets a nice starting point for the user, and also creates potential for more functionality and gave me some welcome design elasticity. The card metaphor was widely understood by the users (who were familiar with the concept from the project management tools they used in tandem with Cable), and it had the flexibility and potential required for the next product iteration.

It also created a visual distinction for state [Needs Reviewing / In Progress / Closed] which allowed me to again reduce complexity, and remove the <filter> component — working my way to remove the extra navbar.

This is the flagship feature and it deserves it’s own space.

Being an iterative step I tried to play it like Lego, moving bricks around without any massive changes, to minimize the engineering time required. There were however some changes that would warrant the engineering effort.

The only thing users were actually engaging with was a database file with individual IDs that needed reviewing. The product solution for this was to allow users to upload a document into the “chat” which was less than ideal. So I added a list component to the UI where the users could see the IDs, and click to copy the ID to clipboard. This list would come to be the most important part of the whole product.

Increasing usefulness

After the initial shake up, it was now possible to start looking deeper into what we were offering to our users, and what should we improve on next.

With the introduction of a Home page and cards, it was immediately obvious from user behavior (and validated through interviews) that both supervisors and managers did a tremendous lot of assigning Priority and Owner to the issues/cards. So we worked to replicate that functionality from inside the Paper Trail page, into the card.

This was again a subtle change, but had a tremendous impact in usability and user engagement.

Proper planning was crucial throughout, but specially in this earlier stage. Because Paper Trails had such a key role, they were connected to almost every initial feature, which meant that changing or adding anything, would likely have an effect elsewhere.

In this case, adding priority to the card meant we needed to add priority to the Paper Trail view as well. It was very important to identify these dependencies and estimate engineering effort accordingly.

Priority indicator

Cable 2.0

Once the correct foundation was in place, the product was able to grow, adding new features and constantly iterating on every aspect of the user experience.

The next big constraint came with the introduction of Oversight — a “super” for governing companies (banks for the most part) to oversee under-management “Programs” (mostly early stage fintechs).

Both the super and the program would be Cable users, with the same functionality and UI, except for Oversight. So when a bank wanted to oversee a given fintech, they’d see the exact same product and UI, with different data.

This required clear visual indicators to avoid confusion as to what “state” the super user was in, and also making sure the product was just as easy to navigate in either mode.

oversight overview

Oversight
requirements

  • At a glance overview of all partnerships health.
  • Ability to group according to certain criteria.
  • Single out a program, and see as they see.

An important piece of this metaphor is the navigation header/bar. The idea is that the user can see the results up front, and the source is hidden behind, easy to glance, easy to interact.

The main use case are banks with multiple fintech startups associated, wanting to see at a glance the overall health of those partnerships — this is different from the banks own fincrime health.

Another requirement was the analysis of particular groupings, or to single out a specific partnership for a more thorough analysis.

Global program stats

Metrics are bespoke to each customer.

Programs list

Tapping a single program will select it for oversight.

Navigation header

Oversight users can use Dashboard, Paper Trails, and Assurance through the lens of their associated programs.

Oversight panel

The user can manipulated this depending on the use case — keeping it all the way up for maximum focus on data, or exposing the full list of programs instead.

Singled out

There’s a lot happening in this view.

Overall, a super user, is using Paper Trails, via Oversight, for Moneygreen’s program.

A lot that went into this feature, but my two main concerns where navigation, and minimizing any chances the user would get confused and mistaken a Paper Trail or other element from a Program, for their own — or vice versa.

I wanted Dashboard, Paper Trails, and Assurance views to be exactly the same as outside of Oversight, both for familiarity and to avoid building out a whole new feature that does the same as something we already have.

Visually, I peppered the UI with cues such as the fintech logo next to the secondary navigation. as well as on the cards (which required another redesign of the cards). The main sidebar navigation also reinforced this.

However, this wasn’t working.

I knew I was pushing the current design beyond its capability and to execute the vision for this feature correctly, it required fundamental changes to the current UI structure.

This poor header — all four of them, are doing too much.

A major technical undertaking.

Removing the menu bar was a big deal design-wise, but an ever greater endeavor for the engineering team, as so much of the overall structure was tied to that key element.

For what could be confused as a minor design tweak, the planning, testing, and validating process was very long and involving. The benefits of this change were thoroughly discussed and weighted against other viable options. And ultimately the product team decided this was the next logical step, and it would further advance the UI in a way that would enable further product growth.

Since so much of the code would have to be re-written, I took the opportunity to bundle some other design tweaks at no extra cost to engineering.

This also meant I had to redesign all other screens to fit the new paradigm, starting with the most important one: Paper Trails.

Minimal nav

Testing showed an overwhelming majority usage of the browser’s back button. An opportunity for subtlety.

Recurring trails

A minor detail users had asked for, the ability to see at a glance if it was a first, or repeat paper trail.

Smart tagging

Filtering with tags, enabled a simpler UI and a text based flow that users could copy paste and share.

More functionality

ID lines were still the most used component. With user engagement over 90%.

Dedicated close trail button

Trails still required a comment to close, so this button is disabled if the comment is empty.

Actions

Integrating other parts of the product, directly into Paper Trails. Users can assign preset actions onto a trail.

Enriched ID export

So much happens to the original ID list, users were asking for a way to getting an updated one, from Cable.

3.0 allowed for a lot of new functionality to be added. Some of it was already in the sidelines, waiting for an opportunity to be ushered in.

As a designer, it’s very important to adequately time product features. Not just from a user/product standpoint, but from a buy-in and engineering standpoint as well. A good understanding of the development process and business goals (long, medium, and short term) is crucial, because everything is important for different reasons, to different people, and I should not feel deterred from improving or fixing something I’ve identified, just because it’ll be a hard sell to engineering or management — I’ll still do it (specially if I’m already working “near” the problem) and then just queue it up according to priority. Eventually the time comes.
